# What this vignette covers

A fitted model becomes a map when you apply it to every cell of a raster. Many
of those cells hold landscape conditions that no survey point sampled. There
the model extrapolates, or predicts beyond the data used to fit it. This
vignette answers two questions. Where on your map is the model extrapolating,
and what can you do about it?

You will project the Quick Start model across its landscape with
`kernel_scale.raster()` and `terra::predict()`, then map the cells that fall
outside the surveyed conditions. The last step is clamping, which replaces any
covariate value beyond a chosen limit with the limit itself. Read
`vignette("v01-quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")` first, because this vignette
starts from that fitted model.

# Project the fitted model

## Fit the model

The example uses the counts at 100 survey points and the three landscape layers
from the Quick Start.

```{r fit}
data("landscape_counts")   # counts and one site-level covariate
data("surv_pts")           # survey locations
pts <- vect(surv_pts)      # convert to a terra SpatVector

# Three landscape layers on one grid, in meters
land_rast <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                              package = "multiScaleR"))

# bin = TRUE stores the distance-binned summaries the fast backend needs
inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast, max_D = 1700,
                      kernel = "gaussian", bin = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)

df    <- data.frame(landscape_counts, inputs$kernel_dat)
start <- glm(counts ~ site + land1 + land2, family = poisson(), data = df)

# Estimate the scales of effect and the coefficients
fit <- multiScale_optim(start, inputs, backend = "profile_glm",
                        n_cores = 1, verbose = FALSE)

round(fit$scale_est)       # sigma and its standard error, in meters
```

The `profile_glm` backend keeps this vignette fast. A model fitted with the
default backend projects in exactly the same way.

## Apply the fitted kernels to the raster

`kernel_scale.raster()` smooths each landscape layer with its fitted kernel, so
every cell holds the value a survey point at that location would have received.
With `scale_center = TRUE` it then standardizes each layer with the mean and
standard deviation from the survey points. The model was fitted to standardized
covariates, and it needs the raster on that same scale.

```{r project-unclamped}
r_unclamped <- kernel_scale.raster(
  raster_stack = land_rast,
  multiScaleR  = fit,       # supplies the fitted kernels and the scaling
  scale_center = TRUE,      # standardize as the model data were standardized
  clamp        = FALSE,     # leave every value as computed
  verbose      = FALSE
)
r_unclamped
```

**How to read the output:** The result has one layer per model covariate.
`land1` and `land2` are in standard deviation units of the survey data, so zero
is the average survey point and a value of 2 is two standard deviations above
it. `land3` is absent because the model does not use it. The `site` layer is a
placeholder. `site` was measured at the survey points and has no raster, so the
function fills a layer with zeros, which is the mean of `site` in these data.
To map a different value, pass it through `site_values`, for example
`site_values = list(site = 1)`.

## Predict the expected count

```{r predict-unclamped, fig.cap = "***Expected count from the unclamped projection, with survey points.***"}
# Expected count in every raster cell
pred_unclamped <- terra::predict(r_unclamped, fit$opt_mod, type = "response")

plot(pred_unclamped, main = "Expected count, unclamped")
points(pts, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "red")
```

```{r count-range}
# Largest expected count on the map and at the survey points
c(map = minmax(pred_unclamped)[2], survey_points = max(fitted(fit$opt_mod)))
```

**How to read this map:** Each cell shows the count the model expects from one
survey at that location, at an average value of `site`. The largest expected
count at any survey point is `r round(max(fitted(fit$opt_mod)), 1)`. The map
reaches `r round(minmax(pred_unclamped)[2], 1)`, which is
`r round(minmax(pred_unclamped)[2] / max(fitted(fit$opt_mod)), 1)` times
higher. No survey supports a count that large. The model produced it by
extending its fitted trend into conditions it never saw.

# Find where the map extrapolates

A cell is an extrapolation when its covariate value lies outside the range of
values at the survey points. Compare the two ranges directly.

```{r compare-ranges}
covs <- c("land1", "land2")

# Range of each covariate at the survey points (row 1 = min, row 2 = max)
lim <- sapply(fit$opt_mod$model[covs], range)

# Range of each covariate across the whole raster
full <- minmax(r_unclamped[[covs]])

range_tab <- data.frame(
  covariate  = covs,
  survey_min = lim[1, ], survey_max = lim[2, ],
  raster_min = full[1, ], raster_max = full[2, ]
)
knitr::kable(range_tab, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r map-outside, fig.cap = "***Cells where at least one covariate lies outside the range at the survey points (yellow), with survey points.***"}
# TRUE where a covariate is below the survey minimum or above the maximum
out_land1 <- r_unclamped$land1 < lim[1, "land1"] |
             r_unclamped$land1 > lim[2, "land1"]
out_land2 <- r_unclamped$land2 < lim[1, "land2"] |
             r_unclamped$land2 > lim[2, "land2"]
outside   <- out_land1 | out_land2

plot(outside, main = "Outside the surveyed range")
points(pts, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "red")

# Percent of cells outside the range: either covariate, then each one
pct_out <- 100 * global(c(outside, out_land1, out_land2), "mean")[, 1]
names(pct_out) <- c("either", "land1", "land2")
round(pct_out, 1)
```

**How to read the table and map:** At the survey points, `land1` spans
`r sprintf("%.2f", lim[1, "land1"])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", lim[2, "land1"])`
standard deviation units. Across the raster it spans
`r sprintf("%.2f", full[1, "land1"])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", full[2, "land1"])`, so some cells have less habitat around them
than any survey point did, and others have more. `land2` shows the same pattern. The
yellow cells make up `r round(pct_out["either"])`% of the map. Every
prediction there is an extrapolation, and the survey data cannot tell you
whether it is right. Most of the yellow area lies along the map border, beyond
the outermost survey points. A few patches sit among the survey points, so a
grid that surrounds an area has not necessarily sampled its conditions.

> **What this means for your study.** Extrapolation compounds under a log
> link. In this Poisson model each additional standard deviation of `land2`
> multiplies the expected count by
> `r round(exp(coef(fit$opt_mod)["land2"]), 2)`, and the multiplication
> continues past the last survey point. Map the cells outside the surveyed
> range before you interpret any projected surface.

# Clamp the covariates to the surveyed range

Clamping acts on the standardized covariate layers before prediction. With
`clamp = TRUE`, a cell below the survey minimum is set to that minimum and a
cell above the survey maximum is set to that maximum. Cells inside the range
keep their values. Clamping applies only when `scale_center = TRUE`.

```{r project-clamped, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "***Left, expected count from the clamped projection. Right, the clamped prediction divided by the unclamped prediction.***"}
r_clamped <- kernel_scale.raster(
  raster_stack = land_rast,
  multiScaleR  = fit,
  scale_center = TRUE,
  clamp        = TRUE,      # hold values at the surveyed minimum and maximum
  verbose      = FALSE
)
pred_clamped <- terra::predict(r_clamped, fit$opt_mod, type = "response")

# Ratio of the two predictions: 1 means clamping changed nothing
change <- pred_clamped / pred_unclamped

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(pred_clamped, main = "Expected count, clamped")
plot(change, main = "Clamped / unclamped")
par(op)

# Smallest and largest ratio, and the new largest expected count
round(c(min_ratio = minmax(change)[1], max_ratio = minmax(change)[2],
        max_count = minmax(pred_clamped)[2]), 2)
```

**How to read these maps:** The left panel is the clamped prediction. The right
panel shows what clamping changed. A ratio of 1 means no change, and that holds
for every cell inside the surveyed range. Ratios below 1 mark cells where
clamping lowered the expected count, by as much as
`r round(100 * (1 - minmax(change)[1]))`%. Ratios above 1 mark cells where it
raised a count that extrapolation had lowered, by a factor of up to `r round(minmax(change)[2], 2)`. The largest expected count on the map
fell from `r round(minmax(pred_unclamped)[2], 1)` to
`r round(minmax(pred_clamped)[2], 1)`.

The clamped maximum still exceeds the largest fitted count at a survey point.
Clamping limits each covariate separately. The cell with the largest clamped
count sits on the western border, where `land1` is held at its survey minimum
and `land2` at its survey maximum. Each value occurred at some survey point,
but no survey point had both.

> **What this means for your study.** Clamping keeps a prediction from running
> away. It does not make the prediction correct. A clamped cell reports what
> the model expects at the edge of the surveyed conditions, which is a
> placeholder for a place you did not sample. Show the map of cells outside the
> surveyed range next to any projected surface, and treat those cells as
> unsupported.

# Move the limits with `pct_mx`

`pct_mx` moves both clamping limits. It takes a value greater than -0.5 and no
larger than 0.99. Each limit moves outward by `pct_mx` times the observed range of that
covariate at the survey points. A positive value widens the allowed range and
permits some extrapolation. A negative value narrows it, so cells near the
edge of the surveyed range are clamped as well. The default, `pct_mx = 0`, uses
the observed minimum and maximum. For `land1` the observed range is
`r round(diff(lim[, "land1"]), 2)` standard deviation units, so `pct_mx = 0.1`
places each limit `r round(0.1 * diff(lim[, "land1"]), 2)` units beyond the
observed value and `pct_mx = -0.1` places it the same distance inside.

```{r pct-mx}
# Narrower limits: each one moves inward
r_narrow <- kernel_scale.raster(land_rast, multiScaleR = fit,
                                scale_center = TRUE, clamp = TRUE,
                                pct_mx = -0.1, verbose = FALSE)

# Wider limits: each one moves outward
r_wide   <- kernel_scale.raster(land_rast, multiScaleR = fit,
                                scale_center = TRUE, clamp = TRUE,
                                pct_mx = 0.1, verbose = FALSE)

pred_narrow <- terra::predict(r_narrow, fit$opt_mod, type = "response")
pred_wide   <- terra::predict(r_wide,   fit$opt_mod, type = "response")

# For each setting: the limits in force, the percent of cells clamped,
# and the largest expected count
layers <- list(r_narrow, r_clamped, r_wide)
preds  <- list(pred_narrow, pred_clamped, pred_wide)
pct_tab <- data.frame(
  pct_mx      = c(-0.1, 0, 0.1),
  land1_lower = sapply(layers, function(r) minmax(r$land1)[1]),
  land1_upper = sapply(layers, function(r) minmax(r$land1)[2]),
  land2_lower = sapply(layers, function(r) minmax(r$land2)[1]),
  land2_upper = sapply(layers, function(r) minmax(r$land2)[2]),
  pct_clamped = sapply(layers, function(r) {
    changed <- r$land1 != r_unclamped$land1 | r$land2 != r_unclamped$land2
    100 * global(changed, "mean")[1, 1]
  }),
  max_count   = sapply(preds, function(p) minmax(p)[2])
)
knitr::kable(pct_tab, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

**How to read the table:** Each row is one setting. The four limit columns give
the smallest and largest value left in each covariate layer, in standard
deviation units, and these are the clamping limits in force. `pct_clamped` is
the percent of raster cells whose value was replaced, and `max_count` is the
largest expected count on the resulting map. Reading down the table, the limits
move apart, fewer cells are clamped, and the largest expected count rises
toward the unclamped value of `r round(minmax(pred_unclamped)[2], 1)`. The
middle row matches the map in the previous section.

A negative `pct_mx` changes cells that lie inside the surveyed range, so it
removes real variation from the map along with the extrapolation. Use it when
the most extreme survey points are few and you do not trust the model at those
values. A positive `pct_mx` accepts the fitted trend a short distance past the
data, which is reasonable only when you expect the relationship to continue
there.

# Choose a setting

| Your situation | Suggested setting |
|:---------------|:------------------|
| Few or no cells fall outside the surveyed range | Clamping changes little. Either setting of `clamp` gives nearly the same map |
| A noticeable share of cells falls outside the surveyed range | `clamp = TRUE` with `pct_mx = 0`. Report the share and show where those cells are |
| You are projecting to a different landscape or time period | `clamp = TRUE`, and consider a negative `pct_mx`. Interpret cells outside the range with caution |
| The model has a log link | Compare the largest unclamped prediction with the largest fitted value first. Extrapolated predictions grow multiplicatively under this link |

No setting substitutes for survey points that cover the conditions you want to
map. If the area outside the surveyed range is large, the more useful response
is to sample it.

# Quick reference

```{r quick-reference, eval = FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
library(terra)

# 1. Fit the model
data("landscape_counts"); data("surv_pts")
pts       <- vect(surv_pts)
land_rast <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                              package = "multiScaleR"))
inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land_rast, max_D = 1700,
                      kernel = "gaussian", bin = TRUE)
df     <- data.frame(landscape_counts, inputs$kernel_dat)
start  <- glm(counts ~ site + land1 + land2, family = poisson(), data = df)
fit    <- multiScale_optim(start, inputs, backend = "profile_glm", n_cores = 1)

# 2. Project without clamping and predict
r_unclamped <- kernel_scale.raster(land_rast, multiScaleR = fit,
                                   scale_center = TRUE, clamp = FALSE)
pred_unclamped <- terra::predict(r_unclamped, fit$opt_mod, type = "response")

# 3. Map the cells outside the surveyed range
covs <- c("land1", "land2")
lim  <- sapply(fit$opt_mod$model[covs], range)     # survey min and max
out_land1 <- r_unclamped$land1 < lim[1, "land1"] |
             r_unclamped$land1 > lim[2, "land1"]
out_land2 <- r_unclamped$land2 < lim[1, "land2"] |
             r_unclamped$land2 > lim[2, "land2"]
outside   <- out_land1 | out_land2
plot(outside)                                      # where the model extrapolates
100 * global(outside, "mean")[1, 1]                # percent of the map

# 4. Clamp to the surveyed range and predict again
r_clamped <- kernel_scale.raster(land_rast, multiScaleR = fit,
                                 scale_center = TRUE, clamp = TRUE)
pred_clamped <- terra::predict(r_clamped, fit$opt_mod, type = "response")
plot(pred_clamped / pred_unclamped)                # 1 = unchanged by clamping

# 5. Narrow or widen the limits
r_narrow <- kernel_scale.raster(land_rast, multiScaleR = fit,
                                scale_center = TRUE, clamp = TRUE,
                                pct_mx = -0.1)     # limits move inward
r_wide   <- kernel_scale.raster(land_rast, multiScaleR = fit,
                                scale_center = TRUE, clamp = TRUE,
                                pct_mx = 0.1)      # limits move outward
```

## Summary of key functions

| Function | Purpose |
|:---------|:--------|
| `kernel_prep()` | Extract raster values around each survey point and prepare the optimizer inputs |
| `multiScale_optim()` | Estimate sigma for each landscape covariate together with the regression coefficients |
| `kernel_scale.raster()` | Smooth each raster layer with its fitted kernel. `scale_center` standardizes the result, `clamp` holds it within the surveyed range, and `pct_mx` moves the limits |
| `terra::predict()` | Apply the fitted model to the smoothed layers, cell by cell |
| `terra::minmax()`, `terra::global()` | Report the range of a layer and summarize a layer across all cells |
